title: Best Up-Down-Up Stretch
statement:
Call a contiguous slice nums[l..r] an up-down-up stretch if you can pick turning points l < p < q < r so that:

  • nums[l..p] is strictly increasing,
  • nums[p..q] is strictly decreasing,
  • nums[q..r] is strictly increasing.

Each of the three parts has at least two elements, and neighbouring parts share their turning point. Return the largest sum of any up-down-up stretch. The input always contains at least one.

examples.why: Climb 1 → 6, drop to 2, climb 3 → 20. Starting at -10 is allowed but only lowers the sum, so start at 1: 1 + 6 + 2 + 3 + 20.
The last climb must take at least one step (-5 → -4), but it may stop there: 2 + 7 − 5 − 4 = 0. Going on to -3 lowers it.
Two stretches exist: 5 9 1 2 (sum 17) and 1 2 -8 -3 (sum -8). The best one is not the last one.

constraints: At least one up-down-up stretch exists
hints: Fix the left end l. Are the turning points p and q then forced?
Yes: p is where the first climb from l stops, and q is where the following drop stops. That gives an O(n²) scan. To beat it, think about what a stretch ending at index i can look like.

Keep three running bests for stretches ending at i: still in the first climb (at least one step), in the drop, and in the final climb. Each one extends from the previous index's values depending on whether nums[i] went up, down or stayed equal.

explain.intuition:
Read the array once and ask, for each index i, three questions. What is the best sum of a slice ending at i that is still in its first climb (with at least one step up)? Best sum that is in the drop? Best sum that is in the final climb? The last one is a complete stretch, so its best value over all i is the answer.

The step from nums[i−1] to nums[i] decides everything. A step up can start a fresh first climb at i−1 or extend one, and it can extend a final climb or turn a drop into one. A step down can extend a drop or turn a first climb into a drop. An equal step kills all three states. Because the first climb may begin at i−1 fresh, negative starts like the -10 in the first example are dropped automatically. It is a small state machine, like a reducer whose state is three numbers.
steps: For i from 1: if nums[i] > nums[i−1], set up2 = max(up2, down) + nums[i], up1 = max(up1, nums[i−1]) + nums[i], down = −∞.
If nums[i] < nums[i−1], set down = max(down, up1) + nums[i] and up1 = up2 = −∞.
If they are equal, reset all three to −∞.
After each step, ans = max(ans, up2). Return ans.
pitfalls: Making the first climb always start where the previous drop ended. It may start anywhere inside a climbing run; restarting at nums[i−1] drops a bad prefix like -3, -2 in [-3, -2, -1, 5, 0, 1].
Updating up2 from the new down in the same step. Use the old values, or order the updates so each reads the previous index's state.
Treating equal neighbours as part of a climb or drop. Both must be strict, so an equal step ends every open stretch.

solutions.title: Walk from every left end
solutions.idea: For each l, the turning points are forced. Walk right through climb, drop, climb and record the sum whenever you are in the final climb.

solutions.title: Three-state DP
solutions.idea: Track the best sum of a slice ending at i in each phase: first climb, drop, final climb. Each step up, down or flat moves sums between phases.

followups: Return the bounds l and r of the best stretch, not just its sum.
Generalise to a pattern of m alternating climbs and drops. How many states does the DP need?
